text: In a circular orbit, gravity alone provides the centripetal force for a satellite, so GMm/r² = mv²/r, which yields v = √(GM/r). Hence the orbital speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the radius: a slower‑moving satellite in a circular orbit must be farther from Earth. Therefore, if the satellite’s speed decreases and it remains in a circular orbit, its orbital radius increases. Its orbital period, T = 2πr/v, also increases, because the path becomes longer while the speed decreases; this matches Kepler’s third law, T² ∝ r³.
